title: Stoned at Ta'if
hookLine: he walks to Ta'if to seek help, and is mocked and driven out

cards: Mecca has closed its doors. The wife who held him is buried. The uncle who shielded him is buried.
So he does something that takes nerve: he leaves, on foot, for Ta'if, a town in the hills, to ask its tribe, Thaqif, for help and a hearing. No army, no escort of clan, no promise of welcome.
He's going to knock on the doors of strangers and say what he has said in Mecca. Today: Ta'if.

teach.b: Ibn Ishaq says he went to the leaders of Thaqif, three brothers, sat with them and told them why he'd come. Their answers are sharp. One says, in effect, if God sent you, I'll tear the covering of the Ka'ba.

Another: couldn't God find anyone but you to send? The third: I won't speak to you at all. If you're really a messenger, you're too great for me to answer, and if you're lying, you're not worth answering.
He gets up and asks them one thing: then keep this between us. They don't.

They stir up the people of the town, and, as the accounts tell it, a crowd follows him out, jeering and shouting, and in some tellings throwing stones, until he reaches an orchard outside town and takes shelter by its wall.
Sahih al-Bukhari keeps his own words about a day like this. Years later, Aisha asks whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud.
He says the worst was the day of al-Aqabah, when he offered himself to Ibn Abd Yalil and was turned away; commentators connect that day with Ta'if.
He went off with his grief, he says, not knowing where he was going, and didn't come to himself until he reached a place called Qarn al-Tha'alib.
The man Muslims honor as the final messenger tells his wife that he walked in a daze. The story doesn't hide it. But notice the verb.
Hurt and dazed, he kept walking. What he said and met along that road is the next few days.

how: Muslims learn the journey to Ta'if as part of the Meccan sirah, retold just before the night journey, and it is remembered when people face rejection.

o: the orchard where he rested after Mecca
the hill town that turned him away
a tribe that sheltered him from Quraysh

games.q: stoned at Ta'if — tap the pairs.
p: I won't speak to you at all
asked about a day harder than Uhud
where he came back to himself

s: he went to Ta'if with a large escort from his clan
the clan's shield was gone; he went to strangers to ask for help.
he later called the Ta'if day harder than the battle of Uhud
the leaders kept his visit quiet as he asked
they stirred up the town, and a crowd drove him out.

games.q: you're him. three leaders have refused you, one with an insult. before you leave, what do you ask?
o: that they at least hear one more argument.
that they keep this between you.
that they give you food for the road.
games.why: Ibn Ishaq says he asked them to keep it quiet. they told the town instead.

practice: Bring to mind one no you've been given lately, a job, an apology not accepted, and let it be as heavy as it is.
Then, if you can, take a few slow steps across the room, feeling each foot land, or, if you can't walk right now, press each foot into the floor in turn.
You don't have to feel better to take the next step, and if you pray, you can bring that no to Allah as it is.

wordCard.voice: Ta'if. The hill town where he went for help, was turned away, mocked and driven out, and kept walking. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the hill town of Thaqif, in the mountains near Mecca.

carryVoice: Your line: he walked on. Not healed yet, just walking. Day seven hundred fifty, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the journey to Ta'if; the three brothers of Thaqif and their replies; the request for secrecy; the crowd; the orchard)
